newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila group says skeletons prove abuses persist.
newsitem.headline: Manila group says skeletons prove abuses persist.

text.p: A Philippine human rights group demanding justice for dissidents missing for years showed on Wednesday the skeletal remains of five Filipinos they said were abducted and killed by security forces.

Two forensic experts who examined the remains of the four men and one woman said the holes most of the skulls bore suggested the victims were shot while at least one was apparently stabbed many times.

The five disappeared within the past 10 years, indicating human rights abuses in the Philippines continued even after the ousting of the late president Ferdinand Marcos in 1986, officials of the Families of Victims of Involuntary Disappearances (FIND) told a news conference.
"Most of the remains tell that the victims suffered brutal deaths," FIND chairwoman Mary Aileen Bacalso said.
"They speak of the truth that amidst the very well manicured Philippines during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum summit, all is not well on the human rights front," she said.
President Fidel Ramos hosted the APEC summit last month in what Manila billed was a grand coming out party of a country that had proved it could achieve economic progress in a democratic environment.

Human Rights Commissioner Vicente Sibulo admitted abuses had occurred even after Marcos was overthrown but data gathered by the state commission showed the number of such cases had significantly declined.
Since Ramos took office in 1992, there have been only isolated cases, Sibulo said by telephone.
FIND officials said they had documented a total of 1,636 cases of unexplained disappearances in the past two decades, most of them occurring during Marcos's 20-year rule.
They gave no figure of cases under the administration of former president Corazon Aquino but said they had confirmed at least 46 disapperances under the Ramos administration.
Most of the victims were peasants, unionists or ordinary people suspected by the military and police of being supporters of the Marxist New People's Army (NPA), human rights activists said.
